newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan unity government still on hold.
newsitem.headline: Angolan unity government still on hold.

text.p: The much-delayed inauguration of an Angolan unity government, now due next week, will not happen until all representatives of the former rebel UNITA movement are in the capital Luanda, diplomats said on Wednesday.

The United Nations appears to be struggling to close the final chapter of a slow-moving peace process to end 19 years of civil war between President Jose Eduardo dos Santos' government and the UNITA rebels.
All but 21 of UNITA's deputies are in the capital but a U.N. Hercules aircraft sent to UNITA's central highlands stronghold on Tuesday to fetch them arrived back empty.

The world body had hoped to have a unity government in place by Saturday when new U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan, who arrived in South Africa on Wednesday, visits Angola for four days -- the first visit since his appointment.
Angola is host to the U.N.'s biggest peacekeeping mission - around 7,000 members overseeing the implementation of a 1994 peace accord.
The inauguration of a national unity government was originally scheduled for January 25, later delayed to March 20, then to next week.

Annan said in Cape Town on Wednesday: "I hope it will be possible that a national unity government will be formed during my visit to Angola. The people of Angola deserve it, they are tired of war and their leaders have to have the courage to give them peace," he said.
It is expected that Annan will express the international community's impatience with the costly drawn-out process.
Western diplomats in the capital said the unity government was not expected soon.
The ruling MPLA's information chief, Joao Lourenco, said this week a date for a unity government had to be set before any swearing in of deputies would take place.
One of the biggest sticking points in the peace process is the role of UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi in the new government.
He still refuses to travel to Luanda and instead prefers to stay close to the UNITA strongholds of Bailundo and Andulo in the centre of the country, for fear of his personal safety.
But diplomats said the two sides had made some progress over the past few weeks in settling on a role for the 62-year-old UNITA chief.
They said a deal making the former guerrilla chief the head of the major opposition party had been agreed to in principle but had not yet been formalised.

A similar deal had been worked out last December before Savimbi met President Nelson Mandela in South Africa. He emerged from the meeting saying he wanted to be part of the unity government instead, possibly an adviser.
"The peace process is at a very critical and delicate moment," U.N. special representative Alioune Blondin Beye told reporters on Tuesday after talks with Savimbi in Bailundo.
"We have to move things forward immediately and all participants in the peace process should act concretely," he added.
The start of the gradual U.N. withdrawal from Angola is scheduled to begin by the end of March with the pullout of 600 Uruguay peacekeepers.
